A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LTC/BLTC research. All 16 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including Appendices A–B, are readable; text and visual inspection support matching equations, experiments and figures across the restructuring.

before.justification: Section 5 and the appendices report original LTC/BLTC compression experiments on synthetic sources and Physics/Speech, including rate-distortion results and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Kodak image-compression comparisons, fixed-rate nested-lattice experiments, runtime measurements and supplementary analyses.

M1.justification: v2 Section 4.2 adds fixed-rate LTC with nested lattices: fine/coarse lattice quantization, coset-index encoding, and a loss combining conditional distortions, estimated overload probability and density fitting. This is a substantive new compression procedure beyond v1's variable-rate LTC and BLTC.

E1.justification: v2 adds large-image compression trained on Vimeo-90k and evaluated on Kodak, substantially extending the earlier synthetic and Physics/Speech coverage. It also evaluates fixed-rate Gaussian coding and low-probability input regions. Banana and Sawbridge were already present in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds reported comparisons with NVTC, VTM and ELIC on Kodak, and with transform-free ECLQ on Gaussian/Banana sources (Table 1 and Figure 23). NVTC was only discussed in v1. The LVQAC-related D_n* experiment compares its quantizer within Cheng2020, rather than evaluating the complete LVQAC system.

E3.justification: New protocols include Cheng2020 image models at four quality levels, PSNR/bpp/BD-rate evaluation, single-core CPU timing, and fixed-rate Gaussian tests with nesting ratios 5, 7 and 9. Table 2 specifies 1024 integration samples for timing. These are added experimental settings, not evidence that the retained low-dimensional experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The earlier lattice-choice, dithering, entropy-model and integration-sample ablations are retained. v2 adds transform-free ECLQ controls, pretrained NTC weights versus trained LTC, low-density-region quantization tests, and rate-dependent Banana case studies (Figures 11–14 and 19–23), substantially expanding the analysis of component roles and generalization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The Monte Carlo integration sample-count analysis is retained; v2's additional averaged runtimes do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for images, nested lattices and new ablations. On Kodak, Table 1 reports -16.708% BD-rate for Cheng2020-LTC-Leech against Cheng2020-NTC; Table 2 reports 8.634 versus 3.241 seconds per image. New Banana results show higher-rate NTC suboptimality and an LTC gap to ECVQ. These are added findings, not same-setting improvements between versions.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.2 introduces nested-lattice definitions, overload probabilities, a conditional-distortion decomposition and the objective in Equations 7–9. It removes v1 Section 2's explicit one-shot-gap bound and reformulates the displayed asymptotic relation for ECLQ. The new printed rate expression also incorrectly equates the log coset count with Gamma raised to the latent dimension.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the emphasis from i.i.d. sequences to sources with intrinsic dimensionality greater than one and a framework incorporating structured coding designs. They add fixed-rate nested-lattice coding and a claim of closing up to 30% of the real-world rate-distortion gap. The abstract now qualifies VQ recovery as approximate.

C2.justification: v1 states that Banana allows no one-shot improvement over NTC; v2 limits this interpretation to low rates and explains the higher-rate gap through two-dimensional quantization geometry. v2 also adds explanations of transform roles and pretrained transfer, fixed-rate performance/complexity tradeoffs, architectural confounding in image comparisons, and limitations of higher-dimensional lattice decoding.

D1.justification: v2 adds the lambda sweep, image quality settings, product-lattice channel arrangement, CVP implementation explanation, image training costs and timing-sample details. The lambda values newly document existing experiments rather than establish a protocol change. The code URL remains in the introduction, but Appendix A inconsistently changes the availability statement to a future release.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around prior neural lattice compression, acknowledging LVQAC as earlier work and distinguishing LTC from LVQAC, LVQ-VAE and Cao et al. It adds analytical support from Shevchenko et al. and nested-lattice background from Zamir et al., while dropping the Li–Gamal one-shot-gap discussion and citation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. Entropy-model discussion is condensed into Section 4.1, results are reorganized around one-shot and block coding, much ablation discussion moves to Appendix B.1, and the conclusion becomes a discussion-and-limitations section. These changes substantially alter the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout and extensively reorganizes displays: v1 Figures 1–2 merge into v2 Figure 1, several Gaussian redundancy plots become rate–SNR views, and Speech/Physics and block-coding figures are consolidated. It adds Kodak/NLQ plots, quantization galleries and two tables, while placing retained ablations in denser appendix panels.

improvement.justification: The Kodak comparisons with matched Cheng2020 variants and measured runtimes address v1's limited practical-scale validation. New transform/pretraining controls and the corrected Banana optimality interpretation substantially strengthen the explanation of when LTC helps. These gains outweigh the local nested-rate formula error, removal of useful one-shot-gap analysis and contradictory code-release wording. The improvement rests on stronger validation and better-qualified conclusions, not simply higher reported performance.
